title: Comparing
goal: Compare two things and name the most — with two endings, ten irregular forms and three comparison patterns used every day.
bekal: name the most with *den beste*, *det største*, *de fleste*
wave: Review **unit 17** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English, and rebuild the dialogue. One question: when *skal*, when *kommer til å*?

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Hvilken by er best?
dialogs.intro: The never-ending debate in Norway, this time at the kitchen table with three cups of coffee and a referee nobody asked for.

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Bergen er den vakreste byen i Norge. Punktum.
lines.id: Bergen is the most beautiful city in Norway. Period.
lines.literal: Bergen is the most-beautiful city-the in Norway. period.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Bergen er våtere enn alle andre byer. Det er noe annet.
lines.id: Bergen is wetter than any other city. That's something else.
lines.literal: Bergen is wetter than all other cities. that is something else.

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Regn gjør en by mer interessant.
lines.id: Rain makes a city more interesting.
lines.literal: rain makes a city more interesting.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Nei, mye mindre. Oslo er størst, Bergen er nummer to.
lines.id: No, much smaller. Oslo is the biggest, Bergen is number two.
lines.literal: no, much smaller. Oslo is biggest, Bergen is number two.

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Rundt sju hundre tusen. Mindre enn de fleste byene du kjenner.
lines.id: About seven hundred thousand. Smaller than most cities you know.
lines.literal: about seven hundred thousand. smaller than the most cities-the you know.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jakarta er ti ganger større. Men Oslo er renere og roligere.
lines.id: Jakarta is ten times bigger. But Oslo is cleaner and calmer.
lines.literal: Jakarta is ten times bigger. but Oslo is cleaner and calmer.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mye dyrere. Men lønna er også høyere.
lines.id: Much more expensive. But the salaries are higher too.
lines.literal: much more-expensive. but salary-the is also higher.

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Er været like dårlig i Jakarta?
lines.id: Is the weather just as bad in Jakarta?
lines.literal: is weather-the equally bad in Jakarta?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Det er ikke så kaldt som her. Men det regner like mye.
lines.id: It's not as cold as here. But it rains just as much.
lines.literal: it is not so cold as here. but it rains equally much.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Da føler du deg hjemme i Bergen, i hvert fall.
lines.id: Then you'd feel right at home in Bergen, anyway.
lines.literal: then feel you yourself at-home in Bergen, in every case.

notes: **Two endings cover almost everything: *-ere* for "more" and *-est* for "most".** *våt → våtere → våtest*, *ren → renere → renest*, *billig → billigere → billigst*. The pattern is just like English *-er/-est*, and just as easy.
**The comparing word is *enn*, not *som*.** *Større **enn** Oslo* — bigger **than** Oslo. *Som* means "as" and belongs in *like … som* (as … as); mixing the two up is a classic beginner mistake.

**There are ten irregular forms, and all of them are common**: *god → bedre → best*, *stor → større → størst*, *liten → mindre → minst*, *mange → flere → flest*. The rest are in the table on the next page.

**Long adjectives use *mer* and *mest*** instead of endings: *mer interessant*, *mest imponerende*. The cutoff is roughly three syllables, and all adjectives borrowed from other languages join this group — much like English "more interesting".

**Like … som** means "as … as": *like dårlig som* (as bad as). The negative is *ikke så … som* (not as … as): *ikke så kaldt som her*. These two patterns are used constantly and are worth learning whole.
**Den vakreste byen** uses double definiteness from unit 12 — *den* in front, the *-e* ending on the superlative, and the ending on the noun. The superlative almost always appears like this.

grammars.title: Three degrees
body: The second form never changes with the noun's gender. The third form changes when there's a definite marker in front.
after: Adjectives ending in *-ig* and *-som* take just *-st*, without *e*: *billigst*, *roligst*, *morsomst*.
Adjectives ending in *-el*, *-en*, *-er* drop the middle *e*: *vakker → vakrere → vakrest*, *sulten → sultnere*.

The superlative **without** a definite marker is used after *er*: *Oslo er størst*. With the marker, it's used in front of a noun: *den største byen*. Both are correct; they just go in different places.

grammars.title: Ten irregular forms
body: These are all words you use every day, so learn them in one go — after that, comparing is practically done.
after: Six of the ten have exact twins in English: *good–better–best*, *bad–worse–worst*, *many–more–most*, *old–elder–eldest*, *young–younger–youngest*, *long–longer–longest*. Since you know English, most of this list is already in place.
⚠️ *Lengre* means "longer" (size), while *lenger* means "longer" (time). One letter apart, and Norwegians themselves often mix them up in writing.
*Mindre* does two jobs: "smaller" and "less". *Mindre penger* = less money.

grammars.title: Three comparison patterns
body: Learn all three as blocks. They come up in almost every conversation that runs longer than ten sentences.

head: Pattern
Example
English
rows: Bergen is as big as Trondheim.
*Det er ikke så kaldt som her.*
It's not as cold as here.
Much more expensive. A little better.

after: ⚠️ One more pattern worth knowing: *jo mer jeg leser, desto bedre forstår jeg* (the more I read, the better I understand). Notice that the second part is **inverted** (*desto bedre forstår jeg*), just like a main clause after a subordinate clause in unit 18. It sounds educated and is very useful for the written exam.
*Mye* is used to strengthen a comparative (*mye bedre* — much better), not *veldig*. *Veldig bedre* is wrong, just like "very better" in English; say *mye bedre* or *litt bedre*.

blocks.text: Comparing almost always ends in giving an opinion, so this vocabulary completes it.

⚠️ **Å synes versus å tro.** English uses "I think" for both. *Synes* is for a personal opinion about taste or value (*jeg synes maten er god*); *tror* is for a guess about facts (*jeg tror han kommer*). Swapping them doesn't make the sentence wrong, but Norwegians hear it immediately.

*Det kommer an på* (it depends) is one of the most used phrases in all of Norwegian, and it has spawned a national joke: whenever a Norwegian is asked to choose between two things, the answer starts there.

sections.title: Eye training: three degrees in a row

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Compare your hometown with Oslo in ten sentences: size, prices, weather, crowds, food, distances, salaries, noise, cleanliness, pace.
Then redo all ten with *like … som* and *ikke så … som*. Notice that the adjective goes back to its base form in both patterns.
Finally, name five "most" things in your life — *den beste boka*, *den lengste reisen*, *det vanskeligste ordet* — with full double definiteness.

vocab.en: to be correct, to add up

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with *enn*, *som* or *så*.
items: Oslo er like stor ____ Bergen? Nei.
Det er ikke ____ kaldt som her.

It's not as cold as here.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: her / kaldt / ikke / som / så / det / er

answers: billigere / billigst — kaldere / kaldest — bedre / best — større / størst — mindre / minst — eldre / eldst
